chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Salih ibn al-Sindi, from Ja'far ibn Bashir, from Mansur ibn Hazim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Three [actions] are responded to with the plural response, even if the person is alone: when one sneezes, it is said, 'May Allah have mercy on you all,' even if there is no one else with him; and when a man greets another man, saying, 'Peace be upon you all,' and when a man supplicates for another man, saying, 'May Allah grant you well-being,' even if he is alone, for there are others [angels] with him.

key_terms.عَافَاكُمُ اللَّهُ: May Allah grant you well-being (plural supplication)
key_terms.غَيْرُهُ: Others (referring to angels or unseen companions)

ai.seo_question: Why is the plural form used when addressing a single person in Islamic etiquette?
ai.summary: In Shia jurisprudence, this hadith from al-Kafi establishes the grammatical principle of 'plural for the single' (al-jama' li-l-wahid) in social etiquette, rooted in the belief that unseen entities like angels accompany the individual. It specifically applies to responses to sneezing, greetings, and supplications, emphasizing that the plural verb or pronoun acknowledges the presence of these spiritual witnesses alongside the person addressed.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Salih Bin Al Sindy, from Ja’far Bin Bashir, from Mansour Bin Hazim, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said:

‘Three would be responded upon by the plural response, and even though it may be one (person only) – during the sneeze it is said, ‘May Allah<sup>azwj</sup> have Mercy on you all’, and even if there does not happen to be someone else with him; and the man greets upon the man, so he is saying, ‘The greetings be upon you all’, and the man supplicating for the man, so he is saying, ‘May Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Grant good health to you all’, and even if he is alone; for there are others (Angels) with him’.
en.sarwar: 10. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Salih ibn al-Sindi from Ja’far ibn Bashir from Mansur ibn Hazim from abu ‘Abd Allah (a.s.) who has said the following: “In three cases the ‘greeting’ is answered in a plural case even if there is only one person: for one’s sneezing, it is said, ‘May Allah grant you (plural) favor.’ when a man offers the ‘greeting of peace’ saying, ‘(I offer you to) be in peace’, the answer is ‘(I offer you to) be in peace,’ and when a man pleads before Allah for good health for another man, he should say, ‘May Allah grant you (plural) good health, even if there is only one person; there are others with him (the guarding angels).”’
